title: Stone That Grows Stronger in the Sea

passage.title: Stone That Grows Stronger in the Sea
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Passage
passage.text:
Along the coast of Italy, giant stone piers built by old Roman builders still stand in the rough surf. For two thousand years, salt waves have hit these harbor walls day and night. Yet the old stone mix stays firm and solid. In contrast, many modern concrete piers start to crack and break after just fifty years in sea water. For a long time, teams wondered why Roman sea walls outlasted modern mixes.

Modern concrete is made by mixing gray cement paste with sand and crushed rock. Inside a modern pier, steel rods are often added for strength. Yet salty sea water seeps into tiny pores in the wall. The salt rusts the steel rods and makes them swell. Within a few decades, that internal swelling pushes the concrete apart from the inside. Before long, waves wash away the cracked outer chunks.

Roman builders used a very different plan near the Bay of Naples. Instead of using plain sand, they mixed white lime with dark ash scooped from volcanic hills. Then they packed that mortar around fist-sized chunks of dark rock and sank the blocks into the bay. For centuries, historians assumed this volcanic mix simply resisted water well. Only when teams checked drilled core samples under strong x-ray beams did the real secret come out.

Rather than breaking the Roman concrete down, the seawater was actually helping it grow stronger. As sea water soaked through tiny pockets in the wall, it melted bits of ash and lime. Microscopic mineral crystals, formed inside tiny pores by seawater reacting with volcanic ash, were steadily grown by the ancient harbor walls over hundreds of years. These interlocking plates acted like tiny stone splints. Whenever a wave caused a hairline crack, new crystals grew right across the gap and sealed it shut.

Today, builders are testing new mixes based on this old mortar. By replacing part of today's cement with volcanic rock dust or fly ash, builders can craft seawalls that heal their own cracks in salt water. Learning how old Romans worked with nature is helping coastal towns build greener, stronger harbors for the future.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 4:

"Microscopic mineral crystals, formed inside tiny pores by seawater reacting with volcanic ash, were steadily grown by the ancient harbor walls over hundreds of years."

Based on the sentence structure, what chemical reaction formed the crystals, and what structure grew them over time?

options.text: The ancient harbor walls formed the seawater, and tiny pores grew the volcanic craters.
options.childFeedback: This scrambles the sentence! Harbor walls didn't form the ocean water, and tiny pores didn't grow volcanoes—seawater and volcanic ash formed crystals inside the walls.

options.text: Roman engineers painted mineral crystals onto steel rods to keep them from rusting.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 2 says modern piers use steel rods, not ancient Roman ones! In Paragraph 4, crystals grew naturally inside the stone pores without anyone painting rods.

options.text: Microscopic mineral crystals built the ancient harbor walls before the volcano erupted.
options.childFeedback: Roman builders built the harbor walls in Paragraph 3; the mineral crystals didn't build the walls—they grew inside the walls' tiny pores over time.

options.text: Seawater reacting with volcanic ash formed the crystals, and the ancient harbor walls grew them over hundreds of years.
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 4, the first 'by' phrase tells us that seawater reacting with volcanic ash formed the crystals, and the second 'by' phrase shows that the ancient harbor walls grew them over centuries.

questions.provingSentenceText: Microscopic mineral crystals, formed inside tiny pores by seawater reacting with volcanic ash, were steadily grown by the ancient harbor walls over hundreds of years.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 4, the first 'by' phrase tells us that seawater reacting with volcanic ash formed the crystals, and the second 'by' phrase shows that the ancient harbor walls grew them over centuries.
questions.parentExplanation: In this passive sentence, the first 'by' phrase ('by seawater reacting with volcanic ash') explains the reaction that formed the crystals, and the second ('by the ancient harbor walls') names the structure that grew them over centuries.
questions.retryHint: Check both 'by' phrases in Paragraph 4: what reaction formed the crystals inside the pores, and what grew them over hundreds of years?

questions.prompt:
Read these sentences from Paragraph 2:

"Yet salty sea water seeps into tiny pores in the wall. The salt rusts the steel rods and makes them swell. Within a few decades, that internal swelling pushes the concrete apart from the inside."

What does the word internal mean as it is used in Paragraph 2?

options.text: Built by ancient Roman engineers near the Bay of Naples
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 2 is describing modern concrete piers with steel rods, not Roman piers near Naples. 'Internal' tells where the rust swelling happens: on the inside.

options.text: Floating on top of the ocean waves far from the harbor
options.childFeedback: Floating on top of ocean waves is outside the pier, whereas 'internal' describes swelling that pushes the concrete apart from deep inside.

options.text: Happening deep inside the material rather than on the outer surface
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 2, 'internal' means happening deep inside a material rather than on the outside. The end of the sentence gives a direct clue: the swelling pushes the concrete apart 'from the inside.'

options.text: Lasting forever without ever changing shape or size
options.childFeedback: Modern concrete in Paragraph 2 cracks and breaks within a few decades instead of lasting forever. 'Internal' means happening on the inside.

questions.provingSentenceText: Within a few decades, that internal swelling pushes the concrete apart from the inside.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 2, 'internal' means happening deep inside a material rather than on the outside. The end of the sentence gives a direct clue: the swelling pushes the concrete apart 'from the inside.'
questions.parentExplanation: The phrase 'from the inside' at the end of the sentence directly defines 'internal' as occurring within the interior of the concrete pier.
questions.retryHint: Look at the last three words of that sentence in Paragraph 2 to see where the swelling pushes from.

questions.prompt: Based on Paragraph 4, how do the mineral crystals inside Roman concrete stop small cracks from spreading?

options.text: They melt the surrounding volcanic rock into hot liquid lava whenever a wave hits.
options.childFeedback: Cold seawater does not melt concrete into hot liquid lava! Paragraph 4 says seawater dissolves tiny bits of ash and lime to grow mineral crystals.

options.text: They grow right across new hairline cracks like tiny splints and seal the gaps shut.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 4 explains that the interlocking mineral crystals act like tiny stone splints, growing right across new hairline cracks to seal them shut.

options.text: They push all the salty ocean water back out into the middle of the Bay of Naples.
options.childFeedback: The crystals don't push ocean water back into the bay; Paragraph 4 says seawater actually soaks into tiny pockets in the wall to help the crystals grow.

options.text: They turn the inner steel rods into flexible rubber bands that never rust.
options.childFeedback: Roman concrete didn't have steel rods or rubber bands inside it. Instead, Paragraph 4 says mineral crystals grew across tiny cracks like stone splints.

questions.provingSentenceText: Whenever a wave caused a hairline crack, new crystals grew right across the gap and sealed it shut.
questions.childTip: Paragraph 4 explains that the interlocking mineral crystals act like tiny stone splints, growing right across new hairline cracks to seal them shut.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 4 explains that the interlocking crystal plates act like tiny stone splints, growing right across hairline cracks to seal them shut.
questions.retryHint: Look at the last two sentences of Paragraph 4 to see what the interlocking crystal plates do when a wave causes a hairline crack.

options.text: By listing in order every Roman emperor who paid for harbor piers along the coast of Italy

options.childFeedback: The author never says engineers should stop building harbors; in fact, Paragraph 5 shows how today's builders are making stronger seawalls.

options.text: By describing how x-ray machines were invented in laboratories fifty years ago
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 3 only mentions x-ray beams in one sentence to show how scientists studied core samples, not how x-ray machines were invented.

options.text: Volcanic ash can only be found at the bottom of the sea near the Bay of Naples.
